html:
The big picture

AI grew out of centuries of formal reasoning (logic, algorithms, the Turing machine) and went through waves of hype and setback — symbolic programs, expert systems, then neural networks. Today "AI" mostly means deep learning: networks of simple artificial neurons stacked in many layers that learn their own features from data. Different data call for different architectures — CNNs for images (small shared filters), RNNs/LSTMs for sequences (a hidden state carried through time), Transformers for long sequences (self-attention compares every element with every other). Networks learn in three ways: supervised (from labelled examples), unsupervised (structure without labels) and reinforcement learning (from rewards while acting). In robotics, deep networks are strongest at turning raw, high-dimensional sensor data into meaning, while classic filters fuse that information probabilistically — the hybrid approach combines both.

Outline

  • History of AI (brief)
  • Modern AI
  • Examples of AI for robotics
  • Mobile robot navigation with AI

History of AI (brief)

Fundamental societal and scientific developments

  • Ancient mythology.

  • Formal reasoning (mechanisation of human thought):

    • Aristotle → the syllogism (350 BC);
    • Euclid → Elements (300 BC);
    • al-Khwarizmi → algebra (the word algorithm comes from his name) (around 800);
    • Thomas Hobbes: "reasoning is nothing but reckoning" (Leviathan, 1651).
  • Boolean logic (1854) — free Boolean algebra with propositions p and q.
  • Turing machine (Alan Turing, 1936) — any process of mathematical deduction can be carried out by a simple machine.
  • The Golden Age of Science Fiction (1937–1941) still shapes our view of technology as a problem-solver. Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics (see 8 Introduction to Human-Robot Interaction) → the first ethical principles for AI and robotics?

The birth of modern AI

  • Based on scientific advances in mathematics (logic), neurology (discovery of firing neurons), cybernetics ("control and communication in the animal and the machine", N. Wiener), information theory (storage and processing of digital information) and psychology (cognitive models of mental processing and memorisation) — and inspired by science fiction.
  • Goal: create an artificial brain.
  • → Formal declaration of AI as a research field: the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on AI (1956).

The first age of AI (1956–1974)

  • Successful AI programs astounded researchers and the public:

    • ELIZA, the first chatbot (Joseph Weizenbaum);
    • STUDENT (Daniel Bobrow, 1963), solving high-school algebra word problems.

  • First applications to robotics:

    • Shakey (Stanford Research Institute) — the first logical, goal-based agent; translated commands into actions;
    • WABOT-1 (Waseda University, Japan) — the first full-scale intelligent humanoid robot.
  • First neural network: the Mark I Perceptron (Frank Rosenblatt, 1960). The New York Times called it "the embryo of an electronic computer that [the Navy] expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence."

The second age of AI (1980–1987)

  • Expert / knowledge-based systems: focused on knowledge, mimicking experts in their fields; domain-specific, useful and successful in the real world, e.g. XCON (John McDermott, 1980).

  • Neural networks revived:

    • Hopfield network (John Hopfield, 1982) — a recurrent network modelled on the Ising model;
    • backpropagation for training (Geoffrey Hinton);
    • David Rumelhart and James McClelland: Parallel Distributed Processing (1986).
  • Important hardware developments: metal-oxide semiconductors (MOS, Bell Labs); very-large-scale integration → Moore's law.

The third age of AI (1993–2011)

  • Commercial successes and challenges met:

    • neural networks for OCR and speech recognition (Yann LeCun);
    • IBM's Deep Blue beats Garry Kasparov (11 May 1997).

  • DARPA Grand Challenges:

    • Stanley (Stanford) is the first robotic car to finish the 131-mile unrehearsed desert course (2005);
    • CMU wins the Urban Challenge: 55 miles in an urban environment, obeying the rules of the road (2007).

The age of deep learning and big data (2011 – now)

  • The roots of deep learning are much older:

    • Perceptron (Frank Rosenblatt, 1960);
    • first deep, feed-forward, supervised multilayer perceptron (Alexey Ivakhnenko, 1967);
    • first CNN, the "Neocognitron" (Kunihiko Fukushima, 1980);
    • the term "deep learning" for machine learning coined by Rina Dechter (1986);
    • first backpropagation for deep neural networks (Yann LeCun, 1989).

  • The boom of the 2010s was caused by

    • the rise in GPU power and efficient training algorithms;
    • the availability of high-quality annotated data sets;
    • the 2012 ILSVRC (ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge).
ILSVRC yearWinner's top-5 errorTechnique
201028.2 %SVM
201125.8 %SVM
201216.4 %CNN
201311.7 %CNN
20146.7 %CNN

(The slide spells the name "Ivkhanenko".)

Intuition

The 2012 row is the turning point: a CNN (AlexNet) cut the error by about a third in one year, and from then on every winner was a deep network. Nothing fundamentally new had been invented — CNNs and backpropagation were decades old. What changed was data (ImageNet's millions of labelled images) and compute (GPUs) large enough to train deep networks properly. That's why the history slides keep pairing algorithms with hardware.

Modern AI

Taxonomy

(Today) "AI" = deep learning with deep neural networks as building blocks.

Common mistake

Using "AI", "machine learning" and "deep learning" as synonyms. They are nested: every deep-learning system is machine learning, every ML system is AI, but not the reverse. A hand-written rule base (an expert system) is AI without learning; a linear regression is machine learning without depth. Today's everyday use of "AI" means the innermost circle.

Neural networks — biologically inspired

Symbols
  • a_i — the i-th input to the neuron (e.g. the output of a neuron in the previous layer); n — number of inputs
  • w_i — the weight on that input: how strongly it counts (learned in training)
  • b — the bias: a learned offset added before activation
  • \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i w_i — the weighted sum of all inputs
  • \sigma — the activation function (e.g. sigmoid or ReLU) applied to that sum; here not standard deviation
  • x — input vector of the network; h — hidden-layer output; y — network output; W_1, W_2 — weight matrices of the two layers
  • A neural network is built up of layers of neurons that are connected with each other.
  • Each neuron processes input information from other neurons and forwards it to other neurons.
Worked example — what one neuron computes
  1. Inputs and parameters: a = (2, 1), weights w = (0.5, -1), bias b = 0.5.
  2. Weighted sum: z = b + a_1 w_1 + a_2 w_2 = 0.5 + 1 - 1 = 0.5.
  3. Activation: with the sigmoid \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, output \sigma(0.5) \approx 0.62; with ReLU, \max(0, z) = 0.5.
  4. Learning means adjusting w and b so that outputs like this one move towards the desired ones.
Why does every neuron need a nonlinear activation \sigma?

Without it, each layer is just a matrix multiplication, and two matrix multiplications in a row are one matrix multiplication: y = W_2 (W_1 x) = (W_2 W_1)\,x. A hundred linear layers would collapse into a single linear layer and could only learn straight-line (linear) relationships. The nonlinearity between layers is what lets depth add power — stacking bends on bends to approximate curved decision boundaries.

What does "deep" stand for?

  • Deep refers to stacking multiple hidden layers (more than one).
  • Modern network architectures can contain 100 or more hidden layers.

Different levels of abstraction

Deep neural networks learn hierarchical feature representations: on face images, the first hidden layer responds to edges and blobs, the second to parts (eyes, noses), the third to whole face-like patterns.

Tasks, architectures and training types

Basic neural-network architecture types: feed-forward networks, convolutional networks (CNN), recurrent networks (RNN), Transformers, …

Training typeTasks
Supervised learningclassification (e.g. object classification / segmentation); regression (e.g. pose estimation)
Reinforcement learningpath planning; control; strategic decision making
Unsupervised learningdimensionality reduction; clustering

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)

  • Sparse connections between neurons create convolutional kernels: each output neuron is connected to only a few neighbouring inputs (unlike a fully connected layer).
  • → CNNs are ideally suited for image recognition.

  • A CNN combines (LeNet, LeCun et al. 1998):

    • convolutional layers;
    • subsampling for dimensionality reduction;
    • fully connected layers for scoring — the number of outputs matches the number of scoring classes.
  • AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012): input images → … → output class scores; the first layer learned 96 kernels of size 11 \times 11 \times 3.
  • The size and number of filters is defined a priori.
  • The filter parameters are learned.
  • Each learned filter kernel produces one activation map as input for subsequent layers.
  • Common tasks: classification, detection (boxes around objects), segmentation (a label per pixel), keypoints.
Worked example — sizes and parameters of the slide's convolution layer
  1. Output size: a 5 \times 5 filter fits into a 32-wide image at 32 - 5 + 1 = 28 positions per direction (no padding, stride 1) → a 28 \times 28 map. The filter's depth 3 matches the image's 3 colour channels, so each filter gives one map.
  2. Parameters per filter: 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 = 75 weights + 1 bias = 76. Six filters: 456 parameters, output 28 \times 28 \times 6.
  3. Compare with fully connected: one neuron connected to the whole image needs 32 \cdot 32 \cdot 3 = 3072 weights — and you'd need one per output position. The convolution reuses the same 75 weights everywhere.
Why are CNNs so well suited to images?

Two properties of images. Locality: a pixel's meaning depends mostly on its neighbours (an edge is a local pattern), so each neuron needs to look only at a small patch — sparse connections. Translation invariance: an edge or an eye looks the same wherever it is in the picture, so the same detector can be shared across all positions. Sharing cuts parameters by orders of magnitude, which means less data is needed to train and the learned features generalise across the image.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)

  • Challenge: temporal sequences with short- and long-term dependencies.
  • Apply the same fully connected network at each time step (weight sharing).
  • Evolving dependencies are captured in a learnable hidden state h^{(t)}, passed from one step to the next.
  • Common tasks: sequence forecasting, regression, natural language processing.

Long short-term memory networks (LSTM) (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997):

  • Introduced to address the challenge of learning long-term dependencies.
  • → LSTMs introduce self-loops where gradients can flow for long durations.

  • Components:

    • hidden state: short-term memory;
    • cell state: long-term memory;
    • input gate: controls which information is important to save long-term;
    • forget gate: determines which information in the cell state is no longer important;
    • output gate: controls which information contributes to the output.
Why does a plain RNN forget long-range information?

Training sends the error signal backwards through every time step, and at each step it is multiplied by roughly the same factor. A factor a little below 1, applied 100 times, shrinks the signal to almost nothing (vanishing gradient); a little above 1 makes it explode. So a plain RNN can't learn that a word 50 steps back mattered. The LSTM's cell state is a mostly additive path — the forget gate scales it, the input gate adds to it — along which the signal can travel many steps without being repeatedly squashed.

Transformers

  • Developed for sequence-to-sequence tasks, i.e. natural-language tasks such as translation.

  • Motivation — the classic seq2seq pipeline: for each item of the input sequence, an encoder (RNN) produces a context, and a decoder (RNN) produces the output item.

    • → Bottleneck: the context vector for each input item (e.g. word) is processed separately by the decoder, which loses long-term dependencies.

  • Ideas to improve: process all encoded input context vectors at once AND multiply each context vector with a learnable score → the attention mechanism.

    • → better captures long-term dependencies;
    • → still includes RNNs or CNNs as part of the encoder and decoder.
  • Idea — "Attention is all you need" (Vaswani et al., NeurIPS 2017): replace the RNNs with a self-attention mechanism. Encoder block: self-attention → feed-forward. Decoder block: self-attention → encoder–decoder attention → feed-forward.

How does self-attention work?

  • Each element of the input sequence is transformed into 3 learnable embeddings — value, key, query.
  • Self-attention compares all keys with a given query: high scores = high relevance, low scores = low relevance.
  • This is multiplied with the value of each item, so that only relevant items are passed forward.
\text{output of the self-attention layer} = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
Symbols
  • Q — queries: one vector per input item asking "what am I looking for?"
  • K — keys: one vector per item saying "what do I contain?"; K^\top — K transposed, so QK^\top holds the dot product (relevance score) of every query with every key
  • V — values: the information each item passes on
  • d_k — length (dimension) of the key vectors; dividing by \sqrt{d_k} keeps the scores from growing too large
  • \operatorname{softmax} — turns each row of scores into positive weights that sum to 1
  • Common tasks: natural language processing → large language models (e.g. ChatGPT); sequence forecasting; recently also image tasks such as pose estimation and object tracking.
  • Simple illustration: http://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/
Intuition

Self-attention works like a soft database lookup. Each word asks a question (query), each word also carries a label (key) and some content (value). The query is compared with every key (dot products: similar vectors → high score); softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted mix of the values. So "it" in "the robot dropped the box because it was heavy" can pull most of its information from "box". Dividing by \sqrt{d_k} keeps the dot products from growing with the vector length and saturating the softmax.

Worked example — self-attention for two items
  1. Embeddings (d_k = 2): queries Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, keys K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, values V = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \end{pmatrix} (one row per item).
  2. Scores: \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{2}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.71 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.71 \end{pmatrix} — each item's query matches its own key best.
  3. Softmax per row: \frac{e^{0.71}}{e^{0.71} + e^{0}} \approx 0.67 and 0.33 → weights \begin{pmatrix} 0.67 & 0.33 \\ 0.33 & 0.67 \end{pmatrix}.
  4. Mix the values: item 1's output = 0.67 \cdot (10, 0) + 0.33 \cdot (0, 10) \approx (6.7,\ 3.3). Each item keeps mostly its own content but also takes in a third of the other's.

Supervised learning

Network parameters are trained using ground-truth labelled data: the network predicts a label (avocado / apple / banana) for each image, the prediction is compared with the actual label, and the parameters are adjusted to reduce the difference.

Reinforcement learning

  • Learning which actions an intelligent agent should take to maximise its cumulative reward by interacting with the environment.

  • Difference to supervised learning:

    • RL does not need ground-truth information / labelled input–output pairs;
    • errors in the actions (sub-optimal actions) are not explicitly corrected.
  • Balance between exploration (→ gaining new knowledge) and exploitation (→ using knowledge).
Worked example — which training type fits?
  1. Detect insulators in drone images, with 5000 hand-labelled images → supervised (classification/detection).
  2. Estimate an object's 6-DoF pose from a camera image, with ground-truth poses from a motion-capture hall → supervised (regression).
  3. Group thousands of unlabelled laser scans into similar-looking places → unsupervised (clustering).
  4. Teach a quadruped to walk by trying in simulation, rewarded for forward speed and penalised for falling → reinforcement learning.

The question to ask: is the correct answer given for each input (supervised), not given at all (unsupervised), or only judged afterwards through a reward (RL)?

Common mistake

Thinking an RL agent "is told" the right action. It only receives a reward — a score — often delayed (a fall happens long after the bad step that caused it). Working out which earlier actions deserve the credit is the hard part of RL, and it's why the agent must also explore: an agent that only exploits its current best guess never finds out that something else would have scored higher.

Examples of AI for robotics

Key challenges for autonomous robotics

Sensors as key elements for localization and perception

Modern robotic platforms (e.g. a research drone with RTK GPS, stereo camera, IMU, laser rangefinder, onboard computer; a robotic ultrasound arm) carry many sensors to infer information about

  • themselves (proprioceptive sensors);
  • the environment (exteroceptive sensors).

Classic sensor data processing pipeline

  • (Novel) sensor on the robot platform → raw data → pre-processing (e.g. feature extraction with classic computer vision) → processed data → sensor fusion (e.g. a Bayes filter variant) together with other proprioceptive and/or exteroceptive sensors → perception task / state estimation.
  • Example for localization: visual-inertial odometry (camera + IMU).

Motivation for the use of deep neural networks

  • DNNs excel at processing or extracting semantic information from raw sensory data, e.g.:

    • What type of objects are in an image, and where?
    • How far are these objects from the camera?
  • DNNs can discover latent features in noisy raw data, e.g.: what is the initial velocity (from noisy IMU signals)?

Use of deep neural networks — the hybrid approach

Hybrid → best of both worlds:

  • DNN: processing of high-dimensional, raw input data;
  • filter: probabilistic fusion of information.
Why not let one big network do everything, end to end?

A network outputs an answer but no trustworthy statement of how uncertain it is, and it can fail badly on inputs unlike its training data — dangerous in a closed control loop. A Bayes filter (e.g. an EKF) does the opposite well: it tracks uncertainty, combines measurements of different quality by weighting them, and uses a physics model of the motion, so a measurement that contradicts everything else can be detected and rejected (the \chi^2 test in the next example). Letting the DNN do perception and the filter do fusion keeps the network's power while keeping the estimate checkable.

Connection

The filter side is the measurement theory of 9 Measurement and Signal Processing (noise, uncertainty, outliers) carried further; proprioceptive vs. exteroceptive sensors were introduced in 2 Sensors.

Object-relative navigation

(T. Jantos et al. — AIVIO, RA-L 2024; AI-based multi-object relative state estimation, ICRA 2023; PoET, CoRL 2023.)

  • Objectives: accurate relative positioning of a mobile robot / drone with respect to objects of interest. Application: autonomous inspection of critical infrastructure, autonomous tracking of objects.
  • Concept: (1) global navigation to approach the objects of interest, detect the first objects, initialise and fix their reference frames, then disable the global sensor; (2) object-relative navigation — detect and estimate each object's reference frame; (3) global navigation again — re-enable the global sensor and fix its reference frame.

  • Methodology:

    • a novel Pose Estimation Transformer (PoET) estimates the 6-DoF pose relative to multiple objects;
    • fusion with IMU and other sensors in an EKF framework.
  • Results on a benchmark dataset: accurate state estimation (mean RMSE about 10 cm and 10 degrees); outlier rejection through \chi^2 testing in the filter. Fusion with inertial data in the filter enables outlier rejection and improves accuracy and robustness.
  • Adapted for power-pole inspection: sim-to-real training of PoET; optimisation for deployment on edge devices. Test flights in the drone hall and in a real-world scenario.

Planar grasp detection

  • Objectives: estimate planar grasp detections for parallel grippers on 2D images; differentiate between graspable and non-graspable components through Gaussian modelling; application: autonomous grasping of critical components for safe handling.
  • Grasps are represented as rectangles; a Gaussian constraint marks non-graspable objects.

Autonomous hydraulic crane

(R. Dhakate et al., Autonomous Control of Redundant Hydraulic Manipulator Using Reinforcement Learning with Action Feedback, IROS 2022.)

  • Motivation: precise analytical modelling is challenging — and not needed for an AI-based controller.
  • Objectives: automate challenging DDD (dull, dangerous, dirty) tasks in handling raw materials; AI vision to categorise and segment the raw material and its geometry and define optimal grasping poses; AI-based control and path planning for redundant manipulators (5-DoF system inputs for 3-DoF position control + 1-DoF orientation control of the end effector; hydraulic joints).

  • Methods:

    • forward network — maps joint space to task space; an ensemble of 20 dense networks; prediction accuracy about 99.6 %, maximum error 2.5 mm;
    • actuator network — maps the non-linear dynamic relationship between piston displacement and joint angles; a single dense network; accuracy about 99.9 % (main) and 99.4 % (secondary joints);
    • RL agent — learns inverse kinematics in the presence of backlash in the base joint, with the DDPG (Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient) algorithm; reward functions for target goal, joint limits, smooth motion, etc.
  • Results: successful application of the sim-to-real-trained control policy on the real manipulator.
Connection

The forward network learns exactly the forward kinematics of 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics, and the RL agent learns the inverse kinematics — for a redundant manipulator, where a target has many joint solutions, and for hydraulics (3 Actuators) whose behaviour is hard to model analytically.

Executing long-horizon, abstract language instructions with a robot

(Brian Ichter et al., "Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances", CoRL 2022, PMLR 205, 2023 — "SayCan".)

  • Objective: extract knowledge from large language models so a robot can follow high-level textual instructions, and make the LLM aware of the success (or not) of instructions in the real world.
  • Methods: connect the skill policies available on the robot (e.g. trained with RL) with the LLM through a learnable affordance mapping; combine the probability from the language model (usefulness) with the probability from a value function (feasibility).
  • Results: on 101 tasks, a planning success rate of 84 % and an execution success rate of 74 %.
Intuition

The LLM knows what would be useful ("to clean a spill: find a sponge, pick it up, bring it") but not what this robot can do right now; the robot's value functions know what is feasible here ("I can see a sponge and can reach it"). Multiplying the two scores picks the next skill that is both sensible and doable — the language model is grounded in the robot's real abilities.

Mobile robot navigation with AI (course VC 700.204)

  • Learn about modern AI for state estimation and control of a mobile robot.
  • Theory and hands-on (group exercises in class and mini projects).
  • Train your own algorithms using PyTorch.
  • Learn about the Robot Operating System (ROS) and Gazebo Sim.
  • Every winter semester.

Control of Networked Systems research group

  • Research areas: collaborative mobile-robot autonomy in 3D space; state-estimation-aware control and planning; on-board environment perception and decision making; long-term task execution; networked mission planning for multiple agents; machine learning for state estimation and control.
  • Drone hall — one of Europe's largest: area 150\,\mathrm{m^2}, height 10 m, tracked volume over 1300\,\mathrm{m^3}; occlusion-free object tracking at 360 Hz with 45 cameras; steel-concrete floor for heavy ground robots.
  • Outdoor arena.

The future of AI for robotics is … you!
